c.tagline: A French-Pacific city wrapped around the world's largest lagoon.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are scarce and must usually be booked by phone rather than hailed on the street; there is no Uber or ride-hailing app, so most visitors rely on hotel transfers or a rental car.

emergency.note: As in mainland France, dial 15 for medical (SAMU), 17 for police and 18 for fire; 112 works from any mobile phone.

avoid.reason: Civil unrest since 2024 (pro-independence tensions) — roadblocks and flare-ups possible; check advisories

hood_desc: Nouméa's main resort beach, lined with hotels, the aquarium, restaurants and the Palm Beach complex; a breezy windsurf and kite bay that is the default tourist base.
A sheltered swimming beach backed by a strip of bars, clubs and restaurants — the city's nightlife and sundowner hub, walkable to Anse Vata.
The downtown core around the palm-shaded Place des Cocotiers, the Port Moselle municipal market, cathedral and museums; the convenient, walkable heart of the city.
An old hillside residential neighbourhood of colonial houses just above the centre and marina; quiet and local, with harbour views.

water.note: Tap water in Nouméa is treated and safe to drink.

transit.pay: The Tanéo network (formerly Karuïa Bus) is paid with a rechargeable Tanéo card or cash to the driver; a single ride is a few hundred CFP francs. There is no rail, metro or tram.
transit.hours: Buses run mainly daytime and early evening on weekdays with sparse weekend service, so a rental car is far more practical for exploring.
transit.note: Nouméa's only public transport is the Tanéo bus network covering the peninsula and Greater Nouméa; service is limited, so most visitors rely on rental cars, taxis or hotel transfers.

bus: RAI intercity buses to other Grande Terre towns
ferry: Gare Maritime (Betico ferry to Île des Pins & Loyalty Islands)

transit.m: Navette Aéroport shuttle bus to Nouméa centre, about 1 hr

tip.r: Tipping is not part of French/Kanak custom and service is included; rounding up for exceptional service is optional.

food.name: Bougna

places.name: Marche de Port Moselle
places.note: Tribal stalls sell prepared bougna parcels and all the ingredients to make it.

places.name: Le Pandanus
places.note: Casual snack with a changing menu of authentic Caledonian and Kanak cooking.

places.name: Le Nautile
places.note: Blends French technique with Melanesian taro, yam and coconut milk.

food.name: Coconut crab and mangrove crab
food.desc: Huge coconut crab, a rare island delicacy, and the everyday crabe de paletuvier from the mangroves, both usually grilled or done in coconut milk.

places.name: Marche de Port Moselle
places.note: Live crab and the day's shellfish sold under the blue hexagonal roofs.

places.name: Le Roof
places.note: Long-standing over-water restaurant known for lagoon seafood platters.

places.name: Le Nautile
places.note: Cooks crab the Melanesian way, with coconut milk and island roots.

food.name: Blue prawns of New Caledonia
food.desc: The territory's famous crevette bleue, farmed in lagoon-fed ponds, served flambeed in whisky, grilled, or raw with citrus and vanilla.

places.name: Le Roof
places.note: Over-water tables and a menu built around lagoon prawns and fish.

places.name: Marche de Port Moselle
places.note: Buy them raw from the fish hall early, before the good ones go.

places.name: Le 1881
places.note: Classic French cooking using the best local produce, prawns included.

food.name: Poisson cru au lait de coco
food.desc: Raw lagoon fish, usually tuna or mahi-mahi, cured in lime juice then loosened with coconut milk, tomato and cucumber; the Pacific lunch plate.

places.name: Marche de Port Moselle
places.note: Market snack counters serve it with a Melanesian coffee, mornings only.

places.name: Lemon Bay Cafe
places.note: Bright cafe over the bay doing brunch, juices and fresh raw-fish plates.

places.name: Baie des Citrons snack bars
places.note: Row of casual beach snacks selling poisson cru and grilled fish all day.

food.name: Cerf (rusa deer)
food.desc: Introduced rusa deer now roams the Grande Terre in huge numbers; the meat turns up as steak, carpaccio, terrine and smoked sausage.

places.name: Le 1881
places.note: French dining room in a heritage building, strong on Caledonian meat.

places.name: Marche de Port Moselle
places.note: Butchers and charcutiers sell venison sausage and terrine to take away.

places.name: Le Pandanus
places.note: Casual kitchen where venison shows up on the rotating menu.

food.name: Baguettes, croissants and French pastry
food.desc: France in the South Pacific: proper baguettes baked twice a day, croissants, tarts and eclairs, eaten with a tropical fruit or a coffee.

places.name: Marche de Port Moselle
places.note: Bakery stalls sell hot bread from opening and pair it with market coffee.

places.name: Quartier Latin boulangeries
places.note: Neighbourhood bakeries near the centre with queues at breakfast.

places.name: Lemon Bay Cafe
places.note: Late breakfast and brunch spot with pastries, juices and smoothies.

food.name: Number One beer
food.desc: The territory's own lager, brewed in Noumea since the 1970s and drunk ice cold at every beach snack, plus the darker Manta from the same brewery.

places.name: Baie des Citrons snack bars
places.note: The classic sunset beer strip; cold Number One with a plate of frites.

places.name: Le Roof
places.note: Over-water terrace for a beer with the lagoon underneath you.

places.name: Marche de Port Moselle
places.note: Market bars pour local beer alongside the morning coffee crowd.

food.name: Kava at a nakamal
food.desc: Earthy Vanuatu kava root, strained and drunk in coconut-shell bowls at dusk in dimly lit nakamals; numbing, calming and strictly non-alcoholic.

places.name: Vallee du Tir nakamals
places.note: Working-class quarter with several long-running kava bars, busiest after work.

places.name: Riviere Salee nakamals
places.note: Neighbourhood nakamals where the Melanesian and ni-Vanuatu communities gather.

places.name: Magenta nakamals
places.note: Easy-to-reach kava bars near the domestic airport, open from late afternoon.

landmarks: Tjibaou Cultural Centre
Renzo Piano's soaring wooden 'cases' rise from a mangrove peninsula, brilliantly celebrating Kanak culture through art, gardens and architecture.
Anse Vata Beach
Nouméa's glamour beach curves along a breezy bay of kitesurfers and seafront cafés, with sunset strolls toward Duck Island's reef.
Baie des Citrons
A sheltered town beach loved for calm swimming and its buzzing strip of bars and restaurants just steps from the sand.
Ouen Toro Hill
WWII gun emplacements top this 128-meter lookout, delivering the definitive panorama over Nouméa's lagoon, bays and barrier reef.
Place des Cocotiers
The palm-shaded colonial heart of downtown, where flame trees, bandstand and fountain host markets, pétanque and city life since the 1860s.
Aquarium des Lagons
An acclaimed aquarium beside Anse Vata showcasing New Caledonia's UNESCO lagoon, from glowing corals to nautilus and sea snakes.
Île aux Canards (Duck Island)
A five-minute water taxi from Anse Vata lands on a tiny reef islet with an underwater snorkel trail through coral gardens.
Cathédrale Saint-Joseph
Built by convict labor in the 1890s, this twin-towered hilltop cathedral watches over the harbor with stained glass and carved Kanak-influenced woodwork.
Port Moselle Market
Under blue hexagonal roofs by the marina, Nouméa's morning market piles up lagoon fish, tropical fruit, flowers and French pastries.
Parc Zoologique et Forestier Michel Corbasson
Nouméa's zoo and forest park showcasing New Caledonia's endemic wildlife, including cagous and flying foxes, amid walking trails.

train.note: New Caledonia has no passenger rail.

bus.note: No international buses. RAI regional coaches link Nouméa with towns across Grande Terre from the Montravel station.

intl.to: Île des Pins & the Loyalty Islands - Lifou, Maré (New Caledonia) - fast ferry from the Gare Maritime

ferry.note: The Betico 2 fast ferry sails from Nouméa's Gare Maritime to the Île des Pins and the Loyalty Islands (Lifou, Maré); cruise ships also call at the port.

half.name: Îlot Maître
half.blurb: A protected lagoon islet 20 minutes by shuttle boat, ringed by turquoise water and snorkelling.

full.name: Amédée Lighthouse
full.blurb: A full-day lagoon cruise to a historic 19th-century iron lighthouse with snorkelling and a Melanesian show.

full.name: Parc de la Rivière Bleue
full.blurb: A red-earth wilderness park of endemic forest and the flightless cagou bird, about 90 minutes from the city.
